claim: Pseudomonas syringae inflicts leaf spots and cankers on plants globally.
source: Pseudomonas syringae inflicts leaf spots and cankers on plants globally, and its adequate control poses significant challenges.
evidence: This is a general statement about P. syringae pathology that draws from established scientific knowledge about this pathogen.

claim: More than 60 pathovars of P. syringae have been identified.
source: More than 60 pathovars have been identified, which infect almost all economically important crops in the world (Bull et al., 2010; Xin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bull et al., 2010 and Xin et al., 2018.

claim: P. syringae pathovars infect almost all economically important crops in the world.
source: More than 60 pathovars have been identified, which infect almost all economically important crops in the world (Bull et al., 2010; Xin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bull et al., 2010 and Xin et al., 2018.

claim: P. syringae pv. phaseolicola 1448A can cause severe halo blight of common beans (Phaseolus vulgaris).
source: P. syringae pv. phaseolicola 1448A (Psph), one of the classical strains of P. syringae, can cause severe halo blight of common beans (Phaseolus vulgaris), which raises it from a common pathogen to a molecular plant–pathogen bacterium (Arnold et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Arnold et al., 2011.

claim: The natural host plants of P. syringae pv. tomato DC3000 are tomatoes.
source: P. syringae pv. tomato DC3000 (Pst) and P. syringae pv. syringae B728a (Pss) are two other model strains whose natural host plants are tomatoes and beans, respectively (Xin and He, 2013; Monier and Lindow, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Xin and He, 2013 and Monier and Lindow, 2005.

claim: The natural host plants of P. syringae pv. syringae B728a are beans.
source: P. syringae pv. tomato DC3000 (Pst) and P. syringae pv. syringae B728a (Pss) are two other model strains whose natural host plants are tomatoes and beans, respectively (Xin and He, 2013; Monier and Lindow, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Xin and He, 2013 and Monier and Lindow, 2005.

claim: The Type III secretion system (T3SS) is the most important weapon of P. syringae.
source: The most important weapon of P. syringae, and the first to be characterized, is the Type III secretion system (T3SS) encoded by hrp and hrc gene clusters, which are flanked by the conserved effector locus and deliver T3 effectors into host cells (Clarke et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clarke et al., 2010.

claim: The T3SS is encoded by hrp and hrc gene clusters.
source: The most important weapon of P. syringae, and the first to be characterized, is the Type III secretion system (T3SS) encoded by hrp and hrc gene clusters, which are flanked by the conserved effector locus and deliver T3 effectors into host cells (Clarke et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clarke et al., 2010.

claim: The T3SS delivers T3 effectors into host cells.
source: The most important weapon of P. syringae, and the first to be characterized, is the Type III secretion system (T3SS) encoded by hrp and hrc gene clusters, which are flanked by the conserved effector locus and deliver T3 effectors into host cells (Clarke et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clarke et al., 2010.

claim: The expression of T3SS genes is inhibited in nutrient media such as King's B (KB).
source: The expression of T3SS genes is inhibited in nutrient media such as King's B (KB), whereas it is induced in minimal medium or plant cells (Rahme et al., 1992; Xiao et al., 2004; Xiao et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rahme et al., 1992; Xiao et al., 2004; and Xiao et al., 1992.

claim: The expression of T3SS genes is induced in minimal medium or plant cells.
source: The expression of T3SS genes is inhibited in nutrient media such as King's B (KB), whereas it is induced in minimal medium or plant cells (Rahme et al., 1992; Xiao et al., 2004; Xiao et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rahme et al., 1992; Xiao et al., 2004; and Xiao et al., 1992.

claim: The HrpRSL pathway is the primary regulator of the T3SS in P. syringae.
source: The HrpRSL pathway is the primary regulator of the T3SS in P. syringae, with HrpRS activating hrpL expression.
evidence: This is a statement about the regulatory pathway that is supported by the context and subsequent citations.

claim: HrpRS activates hrpL expression.
source: The HrpRSL pathway is the primary regulator of the T3SS in P. syringae, with HrpRS activating hrpL expression.
evidence: This is a statement about the regulatory mechanism that is part of established knowledge.

claim: HrpL binds to the hrp box to induce the translation of downstream T3 effectors.
source: HrpL then binds to the hrp box to induce the translation of downstream T3 effectors (Xiao et al., 1994; Hutcheson et al., 2001; Hendrickson et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Xiao et al., 1994; Hutcheson et al., 2001; and Hendrickson et al., 2000.

claim: HrpRSL impacts motility, biofilm formation, siderophore production, and oxidative stress resistance.
source: HrpRSL also impacts other virulence-related mechanisms, including motility, biofilm formation, siderophore production, and oxidative stress resistance, which are under the control of complicated regulatory networks, allowing P. syringae to infect plants (Haefele and Lindow, 1987; Dasgupta et al., 2003; Deng et al., 2014; Fan et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2021; Shao et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Haefele and Lindow, 1987; Dasgupta et al., 2003; Deng et al., 2014; Fan et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2021; Shao et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2022.

claim: DNA methylation is the primary level of epigenetic regulation in bacteria because prokaryotes lack histones and nucleosomes.
source: In bacteria, DNA methylation is the primary level of epigenetic regulation because these prokaryotes lack the histones and nucleosomes of eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about the differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

claim: Bacterial DNA has three primary forms of methylation: N6-methyladenine (6mA), N4-methylcytosine (4mC), and N5-methylcytosine (5mC).
source: Bacterial DNA has three primary forms of methylation: N6-methyladenine (6mA), N4-methylcytosine (4mC), and N5-methylcytosine (5mC).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about bacterial DNA methylation.

claim: 5mC is the most common type of DNA methylation in eukaryotes.
source: The latter is the most common type in eukaryotes, while 6mA is the dominant form in prokaryotes.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about DNA methylation patterns in different organisms.

claim: 6mA is the dominant form of DNA methylation in prokaryotes.
source: The latter is the most common type in eukaryotes, while 6mA is the dominant form in prokaryotes.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about DNA methylation patterns in different organisms.

claim: DNA methylation in bacteria is mainly the product of methyltransferase (MTase) enzymes.
source: DNA methylation in bacteria is mainly the product of methyltransferase (MTase) enzymes, which transfer a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine to various positions on target bases, depending on the modification (Gold et al., 1963).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gold et al., 1963.

claim: MTases transfer a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine to various positions on target bases.
source: DNA methylation in bacteria is mainly the product of methyltransferase (MTase) enzymes, which transfer a methyl group from S-adenosyl-L-methionine to various positions on target bases, depending on the modification (Gold et al., 1963).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gold et al., 1963.

claim: MTases originate from the restriction–modification (R–M) system.
source: MTases originate from the restriction–modification (R–M) system, which protects bacterial cells from invading DNA by recognizing and cleaving specific unmethylated motifs (Casadesús and Low, 2006; Wion and Casadesús, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Casadesús and Low, 2006 and Wion and Casadesús, 2006.

claim: The R–M system protects bacterial cells from invading DNA by recognizing and cleaving specific unmethylated motifs.
source: MTases originate from the restriction–modification (R–M) system, which protects bacterial cells from invading DNA by recognizing and cleaving specific unmethylated motifs (Casadesús and Low, 2006; Wion and Casadesús, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Casadesús and Low, 2006 and Wion and Casadesús, 2006.

claim: There are three main types of R–M systems: Types I, II, and III.
source: There are three main types of R–M systems, Types I, II, and III, categorized according to the related subunits and the precise site of DNA restriction (Bickle and Krüger, 1993; Loenen et al., 2014a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bickle and Krüger, 1993 and Loenen et al., 2014a.

claim: The Type I R–M system contains three host-specificity determinant (hsd) subunits: restriction (R), modification (M), and specificity (S).
source: The Type I R–M system contains three host-specificity determinant (hsd) subunits, restriction (R), modification (M), and specificity (S), which are encoded by hsdR, hsdM, and hsdS, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about Type I R–M systems.

claim: The HsdMSR system exists in around half of all bacteria and archaea species.
source: Genome sequencing and bioinformatics analyses have revealed that the HsdMSR system exists in around half of all bacteria and archaea species (Loenen et al., 2014a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Loenen et al., 2014a.

claim: SMRT sequencing can detect all three forms of DNA methylation, but particularly 6mA.
source: A new sequencing technology, single-molecule real-time (SMRT) sequencing, can detect all three forms of DNA methylation, but particularly 6mA (Beaulaurier et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Beaulaurier et al., 2019.

claim: SMRT-seq has been applied for complete genome sequencing and insertion sequence profiling in different P. syringae pv. actinidiae (Psa) strains.
source: SMRT-seq has been applied for complete genome sequencing and insertion sequence profiling in different P. syringae pv. actinidiae (Psa) strains (Ho et al., 2019; Poulter et al., 2018; Poulter et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ho et al., 2019; Poulter et al., 2018; and Poulter et al., 2017.

claim: Type I R–M systems and their specific motifs have been identified in P. aeruginosa strain PAO1 and two clinical strains via SMRT-seq.
source: In P. aeruginosa, Type I R–M systems, along with their specific motifs, have been identified in the model strain PAO1 and two clinical strains via SMRT-seq.
evidence: This is a statement that is followed by citations in the next sentence.

claim: MTases in P. aeruginosa are considered to play important roles in virulence or drug resistance.
source: These MTases are considered to play important roles in P. aeruginosa virulence or drug resistance (Doberenz et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Doberenz et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022; and Li et al., 2023.

claim: According to REBASE database prediction, 0–2 Type I R–M systems and 3–4 Type II R–M systems exist in the three pathovars of P. syringae.
source: According to REBASE (Roberts et al., 2023) database prediction, 0–2 Type I R–M systems and 3–4 Type II R–M systems exist in the three pathovars of P. syringae, indicating that Type I is more conserved than Type II in this pathogen (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Roberts et al., 2023 and reference to Supplementary file 1.

claim: Type I R–M systems are more conserved than Type II in P. syringae.
source: According to REBASE (Roberts et al., 2023) database prediction, 0–2 Type I R–M systems and 3–4 Type II R–M systems exist in the three pathovars of P. syringae, indicating that Type I is more conserved than Type II in this pathogen (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the REBASE database prediction data.

claim: In Psph, a total of 3849, 4646, and 1807 nucleotides were significantly identified as being 6mA, 5mC, and 4mC modified, with an interpulse duration ratio (IPD) of >1.5.
source: Our results revealed a total of 10,302 modified bases, of which 3849, 4646, and 1807 nucleotides were significantly identified as being 6mA, 5mC, and 4mC modified, with an interpulse duration ratio (IPD) of >1.5 throughout the genome of Psph (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from SMRT-seq and is shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In Psph, 339 genes harbored all three DNA methylation types.
source: Most genes harbored only 6mA modifications, although 339 genes harbored all three DNA methylation types (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis and is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In Pst, a total of 6002, 2242, and 3514 methylation sites were significantly identified as 6mA, 4mC, and 5mC, respectively, using the same cut-off (IPD >1.5).
source: In Pst, a total of 6002, 2242, and 3514 methylation sites were significantly identified as 6mA, 4mC, and 5mC, respectively, using the same cut-off (IPD >1.5) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from SMRT-seq and is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In Pst, 591 (17.7%) genes exhibited modifications in all three methylation types.
source: Among these modified bases, more genes equipped with all three modification types were detected in Pst than Psph, with 591 (17.7%) genes exhibiting modifications in Pst sequences (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis and is shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The methylome atlas of Pss revealed a lower incidence of methylation than those of Psph and Pst, particularly in terms of 6mA modifications.
source: Additionally, the methylome atlas of Pss revealed a lower incidence of methylation than those of Psph and Pst, particularly in terms of 6mA modifications, which were only seen in 457 significant 6mA occurrences under the same threshold (IPD >1.5) and a total of 2853 and 1438 methylation sites were detected as 5mC and 4mC, respectively (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from SMRT-seq and is shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In Pss, 457 significant 6mA occurrences were detected under the threshold (IPD >1.5).
source: Additionally, the methylome atlas of Pss revealed a lower incidence of methylation than those of Psph and Pst, particularly in terms of 6mA modifications, which were only seen in 457 significant 6mA occurrences under the same threshold (IPD >1.5) and a total of 2853 and 1438 methylation sites were detected as 5mC and 4mC, respectively (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from SMRT-seq and is shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In Pss, a total of 2853 and 1438 methylation sites were detected as 5mC and 4mC, respectively.
source: Additionally, the methylome atlas of Pss revealed a lower incidence of methylation than those of Psph and Pst, particularly in terms of 6mA modifications, which were only seen in 457 significant 6mA occurrences under the same threshold (IPD >1.5) and a total of 2853 and 1438 methylation sites were detected as 5mC and 4mC, respectively (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from SMRT-seq and is shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The majority of modifications occurred in coding sequence (CDS) regions, accounting for at least 80%.
source: The majority of modifications occurred in coding sequence (CDS) regions, accounting for at least 80% (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and less than 20% were in intergenic regions and non-coding RNA (tRNA and rRNA).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis and is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Less than 20% of modifications were in intergenic regions and non-coding RNA (tRNA and rRNA).
source: The majority of modifications occurred in coding sequence (CDS) regions, accounting for at least 80% (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and less than 20% were in intergenic regions and non-coding RNA (tRNA and rRNA).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis and is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Compared with 4mC and 5mC, 6mA was more likely to be in intergenic regions.
source: However, compared with 4mC and 5mC, 6mA was more likely to be in intergenic regions, which suggests that it potentially functions in transcription regulation in P. syringae.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the distribution data of methylation sites.

claim: 6mA in intergenic regions potentially functions in transcription regulation in P. syringae.
source: However, compared with 4mC and 5mC, 6mA was more likely to be in intergenic regions, which suggests that it potentially functions in transcription regulation in P. syringae.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the location of 6mA modifications.

claim: 5mC occurs within CpG sites in CpG islands, which contain higher GC percentages in the human genome.
source: It is known that 5mC occurs within CpG sites in CpG islands, which contain higher GC percentages that is typical in the human genome (Bird, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bird, 2002.

claim: The GC architecture can influence DNA methylation in eukaryotic cells.
source: Additionally, the GC architecture can influence DNA methylation in eukaryotic cells (Gelfman et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gelfman et al., 2013.

claim: The GC contents of 6mA sites were the lowest and the closest to the average GC percentage of P. syringae (58% for Psph and Pst, 59.2% for Pss).
source: Compared with 4mC and 5mC, the GC contents of 6mA sites were the lowest and the closest to the average GC percentage of P. syringae (58% for Psph and Pst, 59.2% for Pss) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis and is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 5mC modification bases had the highest GC content, especially in Pss.
source: In contrast, 5mC modification bases had the highest GC content, especially in Pss (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis and is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 4mC sites in Psph had a higher GC content than those in Psa and Pss.
source: Furthermore, 4mC sites in Psph had a higher GC content than those in Psa and Pss (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis and is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The E. coli MTase Dcm can catalyse the 5′CCWGG3′ motif.
source: For instance, the Escherichia coli MTase Dcm can catalyse the 5′CCWGG3′ motif (Militello et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Militello et al., 2012.

claim: In Spiroplasma sp. strain MQ-1, more than 95% of 5mC modifications are found in high-CG sequences.
source: Furthermore, in Spiroplasma sp. strain MQ-1, more than 95% of 5mC modifications are found in high-CG sequences, which is similar to the pattern in eukaryotes (Nur et al., 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nur et al., 1985.

claim: About 25–45% of methylated genes were conserved in two and three strains.
source: Notably, about 25–45% of methylated genes were conserved in two and three strains.
evidence: This claim is based on comparative analysis of methylation data across the three strains.

claim: 5mC had the highest conservation level (39.1%) among the three methylation types.
source: Interestingly, 5mC had the highest conservation level (39.1%), which might be explained by the rare occurrence of 6mA in Pss.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis and includes a speculative explanation.

claim: An obviously higher degree of conservation was observed in virulence-related genes, including T3SS and alginate biosynthesis-related genes, between Psph and Pst.
source: Conversely, an obviously higher degree of conservation was observed in virulence-related genes, including T3SS and alginate biosynthesis-related genes, between Psph and Pst (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: 739 methylated genes harbored sites for different modification types in the three strains.
source: Additionally, some methylated genes (n = 739) harbored sites for different modification types in the three strains (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis and is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The Cro/CI are important TFs present in phages.
source: The Cro/CI are important TFs present in phages.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about phage transcription factors.

claim: The interaction between Cro and CI affects bacteria immunity status in Enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EHEC) strains.
source: The interaction between Cro and CI affects bacteria immunity status in Enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EHEC) strains (Jin et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jin et al., 2022.

claim: Genes with 6mA modifications exhibited more conserved functional terms between Psph and Pst.
source: In contrast, genes with 6mA modifications exhibited more conserved functional terms between Psph and Pst (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis and is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: At least 21 functional terms were conserved between Psph and Pst for genes with 6mA modifications.
source: Remarkably, notable conservation of functional terms was observed for genes with 6mA modifications, with at least 21 terms conserved between Psph and Pst.
evidence: This claim is based on functional enrichment analysis data.

claim: Conserved functional terms for 6mA-modified genes included ATP binding, catalytic activity, integral component of membrane, transferase activity, and phosphorylation.
source: These terms included ATP binding, catalytic activity, integral component of membrane, transferase activity, and phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is based on functional enrichment analysis data.

claim: In Psph, the top three COG classifications encompassed inorganic ion transport, amino acid transport, and transcription.
source: In Psph, the top three COG classifications encompassed inorganic ion transport, amino acid transport, and transcription (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by COG analysis and is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The abundance of modified genes related to cell wall/membrane/envelope biogenesis (M category) in Pss was lower than that of Psph and Pst.
source: Furthermore, the abundance of modified genes related to cell wall/membrane/envelope biogenesis (M category) in Pss was lower than that of Psph and Pst.
evidence: This claim is based on COG analysis data.

claim: Two 6mA motifs were identified in Psph: CAGCN(6)CTC and RAGTACTY.
source: Using the results of both software packages with corresponding cut-offs, we identified two 6mA motifs in Psph: CAGCN(6)CTC and RAGTACTY (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis using PacBio motif finder and MEME suite, and is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The two 6mA motifs in Psph occurred a total of 2998 and 300 times in double strands.
source: The two motifs occurred a total of 2998 and 300 times in double strands, and more than 98% and 77% of those occurrences were methylated, respectively, revealing the high methylation rates of these two motifs and implying their crucial roles in Psph (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis data and is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: More than 98% and 77% of the occurrences of the two 6mA motifs in Psph were methylated, respectively.
source: The two motifs occurred a total of 2998 and 300 times in double strands, and more than 98% and 77% of those occurrences were methylated, respectively, revealing the high methylation rates of these two motifs and implying their crucial roles in Psph (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis data and is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Three motifs for 6mA and one motif for 4mC were identified in Pst.
source: Three motifs for 6mA and one motif for 4mC were identified in Pst (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis and is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The first 6mA motif in Pst, CAARGAA, was found 2022 times in the genome, with 2019 of the occurrences methylated (99.8%).
source: The first 6mA motif, CAARGAA, was found 2022 times in the genome, with 2019 of the occurrences methylated (99.8%) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis data and is shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The second 6mA motif in Pst, GAAN(4)RTRCC, was fully methylated in both strands.
source: The second 6mA motif, GAAN(4)RTRCC, was fully methylated in both strands.
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis data.

claim: The last 6mA motif in Pst, GYAGN(5)CTRC, exhibited a high methylation level (96%) in the genome.
source: Similarly, the last 6mA motif, GYAGN(5)CTRC, exhibited a high methylation level (96%) in the genome of Pst.
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis data.

claim: The only 4mC motif identified in Pst displayed a considerably lower methylation level than the 6mA sites, with 2207 occurrences of methylation out of a total of 8048 sites (approximately 27%).
source: Conversely, the only motif identified for 4mC in Pst displayed a considerably lower methylation level than the 6mA sites, with 2207 occurrences of methylation out of a total of 8048 sites (approximately 27%).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif analysis data.

claim: No credible motifs were found in Pss because of its noticeably lower modification levels compared with the other two strains.
source: Notably, no credible motifs were found in Pss because of its noticeably lower modification levels compared with the other two strains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lower methylation levels observed in Pss.

claim: The first motif identified in Psph, CAGCN(6)CTC, is similar to the counterpart modified by a Type I R–M MTase in P. aeruginosa.
source: The first motif, CAGCN(6)CTC, identified in Psph is similar to the counterpart modified by a Type I R–M MTase in P. aeruginosa (Beaulaurier et al., 2019; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the putative HsdMSR is responsible for the observed motif.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Beaulaurier et al., 2019 and comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The putative HsdMSR is responsible for the CAGCN(6)CTC motif in Psph.
source: The first motif, CAGCN(6)CTC, identified in Psph is similar to the counterpart modified by a Type I R–M MTase in P. aeruginosa (Beaulaurier et al., 2019; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the putative HsdMSR is responsible for the observed motif.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity to P. aeruginosa motifs.

claim: Growth curve experiments showed adverse effects on ΔhsdMSR compared to the WT strain.
source: Growth curve experiments showed the adverse effects on ΔhsdMSR compared to the WT strain (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: 6mA levels were significantly decreased in ΔhsdMSR compared to the WT, but were restored in the complemented strain.
source: The results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B illustrated that 6mA levels were significantly decreased in ΔhsdMSR compared to the WT, but were restored in the complemented strain.
evidence: This claim is supported by dot blot assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Almost all of the reduction 6mA sites in the ΔhsdMSR were from motif CAGCN(6)CTC.
source: As expected, we found almost all of the reduction 6mA sites in the ΔhsdMSR were from motif CAGCN(6)CTC (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by SMRT-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E, F.

claim: 5mC and 4mC sites in the ΔhsdMSR mutant were relatively similar to that in WT.
source: We also noticed that 5mC and 4mC sites in the mutant were relatively similar to that in WT (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E), and the slight difference might be caused by sequencing errors.
evidence: This claim is supported by SMRT-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: HsdMSR only catalyzes the 6mA located on the motif CAGCN(6)CTC, but does not affect other 6mA sites and other modification types.
source: Overall, we propose that HsdMSR only catalyze the 6mA located on the motif CAGCN(6)CTC, but does not affect other 6mA sites and other modification types.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SMRT-seq data comparing WT and ΔhsdMSR.

claim: Growth conditions affect the bacterial methylation status.
source: In accordance with previous studies showing that growth conditions affect the bacterial methylation status (Gonzalez and Collier, 2013; Krebes et al., 2014; Sánchez-Romero and Casadesús, 2020), we applied dot blot experiments using the same amount of DNA (1 μg) from these three P. syringae strains to detect the 6mA levels during both logarithmic and stationary phases.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gonzalez and Collier, 2013; Krebes et al., 2014; and Sánchez-Romero and Casadesús, 2020.

claim: 6mA levels in the stationary phase were much higher than those in the logarithmic phase in Psph and Pst, but no significant change in Pss.
source: The results revealed that 6mA levels in the stationary phase were much higher than those in the logarithmic phase in Psph and Pst, but no significant change in Pss (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by dot blot assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: During the stationary phase, 6mA methylation levels in Psph and Pst were higher than those in Pss.
source: Additionally, we found that during the stationary phase, 6mA methylation levels in Psph and Pst were higher than those in Pss.
evidence: This claim is supported by dot blot assay data.

claim: Pss does not harbor any Type I R–M systems.
source: These findings were consistent with the MTases predication on these three strains since Pss does not harbor any Type I R–M systems, which are important for 6mA medication in bacteria.
evidence: This is based on REBASE database prediction mentioned earlier in the manuscript.

claim: The MTase overexpressed strain presents a higher 6mA level than WT during the logarithmic phase.
source: The results showed that the MTase overexpressed strain presents a higher 6mA level than WT during the logarithmic phase, and the overexpression of MTase had no effects on growth in Pst (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by dot blot assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The overexpression of MTase had no effects on growth in Pst.
source: The results showed that the MTase overexpressed strain presents a higher 6mA level than WT during the logarithmic phase, and the overexpression of MTase had no effects on growth in Pst (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: 6mA levels change with the bacterial growth phase in Psph and Pst.
source: Taken together, the results demonstrated that 6mA levels change with the bacterial growth phase in Psph and Pst, and HsdMSR is responsible for maintaining 6mA sites within the sequence motif of CAGCN(6)CTC in Psph.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dot blot assay data.

claim: HsdMSR is responsible for maintaining 6mA sites within the sequence motif of CAGCN(6)CTC in Psph.
source: Taken together, the results demonstrated that 6mA levels change with the bacterial growth phase in Psph and Pst, and HsdMSR is responsible for maintaining 6mA sites within the sequence motif of CAGCN(6)CTC in Psph.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SMRT-seq and dot blot assay data.

claim: 395 DEGs were identified between WT and ΔhsdMSR with the cut-off of |log2FC| > 1 and an adjusted p-value <0.05.
source: We identified 395 DEGs between WT and ΔhsdMSR under these experimental conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Among the 395 DEGs, 218 genes were upregulated, while 177 genes were downregulated compared with the WT.
source: Among these, 218 genes were upregulated, while 177 genes were downregulated compared with the WT (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The upregulated functional terms included alginate biosynthesis, fructose and mannose metabolism, and the oxidation–reduction process.
source: When using adjusted p-value <0.05 as a significant cut-off, the upregulated functional terms included alginate biosynthesis, fructose and mannose metabolism, and the oxidation–reduction process (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The downregulated pathways included the citrate cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, ribosome structure, and translation.
source: The downregulated pathways included the citrate cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, ribosome structure, and translation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 116 genes showed bigger differences (|log2FC| > 2) except for genes related to ribosomal protein, T3SS, and alginate synthesis.
source: A total of 116 genes showed bigger differences (|log2FC| > 2) except for genes related to ribosomal protein, T3SS, and alginate synthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Among the 116 genes with |log2FC| > 2, 31 were annotated as hypothetical proteins and 4 as transcription factors with unknown functions.
source: Among these genes, 31 were annotated as hypothetical proteins and 4 as transcription factors with unknown functions, and the remaining genes mostly encoded metabolism-related enzymes.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis and gene annotation.

claim: The upregulated genes were more likely to be involved in lanes E (amino acid transport and metabolism), G (carbohydrate transport and metabolism), and I (lipid transport and metabolism).
source: We also analyzed the function alteration via COG category analysis of DEGs, which revealed that the upregulated genes were more likely to be involved in lanes E (amino acid transport and metabolism), G (carbohydrate transport and metabolism), and I (lipid transport and metabolism) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by COG analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Downregulated DEGs were significantly involved in lanes F (nucleotide transport and metabolism) and J (translation, ribosomal structure, and biogenesis).
source: Downregulated DEGs were significantly involved in lanes F (nucleotide transport and metabolism) and J (translation, ribosomal structure, and biogenesis) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by COG analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: 76 genes overlapped between DEGs and genes harboring the HsdM-recognizing motif.
source: Although the overlap was not statistically significant (p > 0.05), we identified 76 overlapping genes (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Eight DEGs harbored the HsdMSR methylation motif at the putative promoter region (within 100 bp upstream of the gene).
source: Eight DEGs harbored the HsdMSR methylation motif at the putative promoter region (within 100 bp upstream of the gene) (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Supplementary file 4.

claim: Several T3SS effector genes were identified as upregulated, including hopAE1, hrpF, hrpA2, hrpK1, and hrpW1.
source: Several T3SS effector genes were identified as upregulated, including hopAE1, hrpF, hrpA2, hrpK1, and hrpW1.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: The transcriptional levels of all T3SS genes tested were confirmed as being significantly higher in the ΔhsdMSR than the WT by RT-qPCR.
source: RT-qPCR was applied under the same conditions as RNA-seq, and the transcriptional levels of all genes were confirmed as being significantly higher in the ΔhsdMSR than the WT (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Gene expression levels of T3SS genes were restored in the complemented strain.
source: These gene expression levels were restored in the complemented strain.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data.

claim: ΔhsdMSR was observed to induce more severe symptoms than the WT and complemented strains at 6 days post-inoculation in bean plants.
source: At 6 days post-inoculation, ΔhsdMSR was observed to induce more severe symptoms than the WT and complemented strains (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by plant infection assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: HsdMSR inhibited the expression of T3 effectors under KB conditions.
source: Overall, HsdMSR inhibited the expression of T3 effectors under KB conditions, and the loss of this modification system enhanced the pathogenicity of the strain during plant infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RT-qPCR and plant infection assay data.

claim: The loss of HsdMSR enhanced the pathogenicity of the strain during plant infection.
source: Overall, HsdMSR inhibited the expression of T3 effectors under KB conditions, and the loss of this modification system enhanced the pathogenicity of the strain during plant infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the plant infection assay data.

claim: Alginate biosynthesis proteins have been demonstrated to be essential for extracellular polymeric substances production, which enhances biofilm formation during the bacterial infection process.
source: Alginate biosynthesis proteins have been demonstrated to be essential for extracellular polymeric substances production, which enhances biofilm formation during the bacterial infection process (Boyd and Chakrabarty, 1995; Ichinose et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boyd and Chakrabarty, 1995 and Ichinose et al., 2013.

claim: The expression levels of alginate biosynthesis genes (alg8, algE, alg44, algF, and algD) in ΔhsdMSR were significantly increased compared with the WT and complemented strain.
source: The expression levels of these genes in ΔhsdMSR were significantly increased compared with the WT and complemented strain (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The intensity of crystal violet staining of biofilms formed by the WT and complemented strains was significantly less strong than that of ΔhsdMSR cells.
source: The intensity of crystal violet staining of biofilms formed by the WT and complemented strains was significantly less strong than that of ΔhsdMSR cells (Figure 5D), supporting the role of HsdMSR in controlling biofilm formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by crystal violet staining assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: HsdMSR regulates the virulence of P. syringae by tuning its expression of T3SS and alginate biosynthesis genes.
source: We therefore concluded that HsdMSR regulates the virulence of P. syringae by tuning its expression of T3SS and alginate biosynthesis genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RT-qPCR, plant infection assay, and biofilm formation assay data.

claim: Regulation of ribosomal gene expression is essential to the integrity of the ribosome structure, which affects translation.
source: Regulation of ribosomal gene expression is essential to the integrity of the ribosome structure, which affects translation (Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2015.

claim: The low expression level of ribosome proteins in ΔhsdMSR would result in delayed growth.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that the low expression level of ribosome proteins in ΔhsdMSR would result in delayed growth.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the RNA-seq data and established knowledge about ribosomal proteins.

claim: The mRNA expression levels of ribosomal protein genes (rplS, rpmD, rpsS, and rpsJ) were significantly lower in ΔhsdMSR than in WT.
source: The RT-qPCR results demonstrated that the mRNA expression levels of these genes were significantly lower in ΔhsdMSR than in WT, while levels in the complemented strain were restored to the WT level (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The mRNA expression levels of ribosomal protein genes in the complemented strain were restored to the WT level.
source: The RT-qPCR results demonstrated that the mRNA expression levels of these genes were significantly lower in ΔhsdMSR than in WT, while levels in the complemented strain were restored to the WT level (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The TE of 162 genes was significantly different (|log2FC| > 1.5) when comparing the WT and ΔhsdMSR.
source: When we compared the WT and ΔhsdMSR, the TE of 162 genes was significantly different (|log2FC| > 1.5) (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ribo-seq data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Of the 162 genes with significantly different TE, 73 genes had enhanced TE, while 89 had suppressed TE.
source: Of these genes, 73 genes had enhanced TE, while 89 had suppressed TE (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ribo-seq data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Most of the genes with significantly different TE were related to transmembrane transport and transcription regulation.
source: Most of these genes were related to transmembrane transport and transcription regulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The TE of genes linked to the oxidation–reduction process tended to be suppressed.
source: Remarkably, the TE of genes linked to the oxidation–reduction process tended to be suppressed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: HsdMSR plays an important role in the regulation of metabolism by promoting ribosomal protein synthesis and modulating TE in Psph.
source: These results showed that HsdMSR plays an important role in the regulation of metabolism by promoting ribosomal protein synthesis and modulating TE in Psph.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RT-qPCR and Ribo-seq data.

claim: A methylation motif was found in the upstream region of hrpF.
source: Interestingly, we noticed a methylation motif in the upstream region of hrpF (encoding the pathogenicity factor HrpF), which increased its expression level in the Psph WT strain (Figures 5A and 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The hrpF-lux signal in ΔhsdMSR increased along with culture time and reached a peak at 24 hr.
source: The hrpF-lux signal in ΔhsdMSR increased along with culture time and reached a peak at 24 hr when the methylation level was also elevated in the late growth stage (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by lux-reporter assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The lux-reporter assay confirmed that hrpF was remarkably upregulated in ΔhsdMSR compared with the WT strain.
source: This result of the lux-reporter assay confirmed the RNA-seq and RT-qPCR results showing that hrpF was remarkably upregulated in ΔhsdMSR compared with the WT strain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lux-reporter assay data.

claim: A hemi-methylated pattern is insufficient for transcriptional alteration of hrpF.
source: This resulted in a low hrpF expression level similar to that of the WT sequence carrying the A base (Figure 6C), indicating that a hemi-methylated pattern is insufficient for transcriptional alteration.
evidence: This claim is supported by lux-reporter assay data with point mutations shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The reporter carrying the HsdMSR motif without two A bases resulted in a significantly higher signal than the hemi-mutated and non-mutated reporters in the WT.
source: As expected, the reporter carrying the HsdMSR motif without two A bases resulted in a significantly higher signal than the hemi-mutated and non-mutated reporters in the WT (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by lux-reporter assay data with double mutations shown in Figure 6C.

claim: HsdMSR regulation of hrpF transcription was based on both strands being fully methylated.
source: Taken together, the results showed that HsdMSR regulation of hrpF transcription was based on both strands being fully methylated.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lux-reporter assay data with point mutations.

claim: 6mA is the most prevalent modification type in Psph and Pst.
source: Comprehensive analysis of the methylome atlas revealed that 6mA is the most prevalent modification type in Psph and Pst, mirroring the trends observed in other bacteria.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SMRT-seq data analysis.

claim: Pss displays the lowest occurrences of 6mA throughout its genome.
source: Conversely, Pss displays the lowest occurrences of 6mA throughout its genome (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by SMRT-seq data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The absence of the Type I R–M MTase responsible for 6mA in Pss might explain the low occurrences of 6mA.
source: This discrepancy might be attributed to the absence of the Type I R–M MTase responsible for 6mA in Pss.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on the REBASE database prediction and SMRT-seq data.

claim: The presence of two Type I R–M MTases in Pst possibly contributes to it having a higher number of 6mA sites than Psph.
source: Similarly, the presence of two Type I R–M MTases in Pst possibly contribute to it having a higher number of 6mA sites than Psph.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on the REBASE database prediction and SMRT-seq data.

claim: All three pathovars had a similar pattern, with 4mC being the least frequent modification type.
source: Additionally, all three pathovars had a similar pattern, with 4mC being the least frequent modification type.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SMRT-seq data analysis.

claim: The three strains tested displayed remarkably divergent methylation patterns.
source: Despite belonging to the same P. syringae species, the three strains tested displayed remarkably divergent methylation patterns, which is reminiscent of the phenomenon observed in Xanthomonas spp. (Seong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SMRT-seq data analysis and is compared to observations in Xanthomonas spp.

claim: The 6mA motifs had extremely high methylation levels, ranging from 77% to 100%, in the stationary phase of P. syringae.
source: We found that the 6mA motifs had extremely high methylation levels, ranging from 77% to 100%, in the stationary phase of P. syringae.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the motif analysis data.

claim: The 6mA methylation levels increased during Psph growth, similar to the observations in P. aeruginosa.
source: We subsequently found that the 6mA methylation levels increased during Psph growth, similar to the observations in P. aeruginosa (Doberenz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by dot blot assay data and a citation to Doberenz et al., 2017.

claim: DNA methylation is much more stable under different conditions and growth phases in Helicobacter pylori and Salmonella typhimurium.
source: However, DNA methylation is much more stable under different conditions and growth phases in Helicobacter pylori and Salmonella typhimurium (Krebes et al., 2014; Bourgeois et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Krebes et al., 2014 and Bourgeois et al., 2022.

claim: MTases have been reported to play important roles in bacterial growth.
source: MTases have been reported to play important roles in bacterial growth; for example, they are involved in cell cycle processes such as chromosomal replication in E. coli and Caulobacter crescentus (Reyes-Lamothe and Sherratt, 2019; Gonzalez et al., 2014; Kozdon et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Reyes-Lamothe and Sherratt, 2019; Gonzalez et al., 2014; and Kozdon et al., 2013.

claim: DNA methylation can activate DnaA and signal the initiation of chromosome replication to affect the growth of gamma-proteobacteria.
source: DNA methylation can activate DnaA and signal the initiation of chromosome replication to affect the growth of gamma-proteobacteria (Seong et al., 2021; Boye et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Seong et al., 2021 and Boye et al., 1996.

claim: DNA methylation influences bacterial growth through genes related to diverse carbohydrate transport mechanisms.
source: Previous studies revealed that DNA methylation influences bacterial growth through genes related to diverse carbohydrate transport mechanisms (Park et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Park et al., 2019.

claim: The 6mA modification catalyzed by HsdM in Psph positively affects its growth.
source: We report that the 6mA modification catalyzed by HsdM in Psph positively affects its growth, which can be explained by the downregulation of ribosomal proteins and the alteration of metabolism-related gene TE.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the growth curve, RNA-seq, and Ribo-seq data.

claim: Many MTases are thought to be uncorrelated to growth in bacterial species such as P. aeruginosa and Klebsiella pneumoniae.
source: However, many MTases are thought to be uncorrelated to growth in bacterial species such as P. aeruginosa and Klebsiella pneumoniae (Doberenz et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022; Fang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Doberenz et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022; and Fang et al., 2017.

claim: Many MTases and DNA methylations are involved in bacterial virulence through their modulation of gene expression.
source: Many MTases and DNA methylations are involved in bacterial virulence through their modulation of gene expression (Doberenz et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022; Fang et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2018; Park et al., 2019; Park et al., 2021; Manzer et al., 2023; Banas et al., 2011; Oliveira et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Doberenz et al., 2017; Han et al., 2022; Fang et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2018; Park et al., 2019; Park et al., 2021; Manzer et al., 2023; Banas et al., 2011; Oliveira et al., 2020.

claim: Not all DEGs harbored the HsdMSR methylation motif in their promoter region.
source: Remarkably, not all DEGs harbored the HsdMSR methylation motif in their promoter region.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: There were no significant correlations between the HsdM-recognized motif sites in the promoter region and DEGs.
source: There were no significant correlations between the HsdM-recognized motif sites in the promoter region and DEGs, even though DNA methylation is generally known to affect gene expression by altering the interactions between DNA and proteins such as TFs, which compete with MTases at specific motif sites and thus influence downstream transcription (Lim and van Oudenaarden, 2007).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis, with a citation to Lim and van Oudenaarden, 2007 for context.

claim: DNA methylation within CDS can alter gene expression in bacteria.
source: However, recent studies have revealed that DNA methylation within CDS can also alter gene expression in bacteria; for example, 5mC in CDS can enhance transcription while blocking the transcription of CpG islands in promoters in eukaryotic cells (Kahramanoglou et al., 2012; Rishi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kahramanoglou et al., 2012 and Rishi et al., 2010.

claim: 6mA in Psph can regulate gene expression directly and indirectly.
source: We hypothesize that 6mA in Psph can regulate gene expression directly and indirectly.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the data analysis and literature.

claim: The 6mA motif in the promoter region of hrpF can directly and negatively regulate gene transcription in a manner dependent on full methylation of the strands.
source: We confirmed that the 6mA motif in the promoter region of hrpF can directly and negatively regulate gene transcription in a manner dependent on full methylation of the strands (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by lux-reporter assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: DEGs carrying modified sites, including alginate biosynthesis-related genes and T3 effectors, are believed to be caused by the alteration of nucleoid topology.
source: Therefore, those DEGs carrying modified sites, including alginate biosynthesis-related genes and T3 effectors, are believed to be caused by the alteration of nucleoid topology, as seen in Salmonella and H. pylori (Kumar et al., 2018; Camacho et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to Kumar et al., 2018 and Camacho et al., 2005.

claim: The 6mA sites, including those in virulence-related hrc/hrp and alg genes, are conserved in Psph and Pst.
source: Furthermore, the 6mA sites, including those in virulence-related hrc/hrp and alg genes, are conserved in Psph and Pst, implying that similar phenotypes occur in the latter strain.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis with an inference about phenotypes.

claim: 6mA modifications in Psph act as important epigenetic regulators of gene expression.
source: Altogether, 6mA modifications in Psph were observed to act as important epigenetic regulators of gene expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall data analysis.

claim: The growth phase affects methylation levels in P. syringae.
source: For instance, we confirmed that the growth phase affects methylation levels in P. syringae.
evidence: This claim is supported by dot blot assay data.

claim: Increased temperatures can reduce methylation levels in P. aeruginosa PAO1.
source: Previous studies have shown that increased temperatures can reduce methylation levels, as observed in P. aeruginosa PAO1 (Doberenz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Doberenz et al., 2017.

claim: HsdMSR expression may be responsive to both intrinsic cellular states and extrinsic environmental conditions.
source: These findings suggest that HsdMSR expression may be responsive to both intrinsic cellular states and extrinsic environmental conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the data and literature.

claim: Three candidate TFs (PSPPH_0061, PSPPH_3268, and PSPPH_3504) might directly bind and regulate HsdMSR expression.
source: As a result, we found three candidate TFs (PSPPH_0061, PSPPH_3268, and PSPPH_3504) that might directly bind and regulate HsdMSR expression.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on TF-binding site analysis.

claim: R–M systems are known for their intrinsic role as innate immune systems in anti-phage infection.
source: Moreover, R–M systems are known for their intrinsic role as innate immune systems in anti-phage infection, and present in around 90% of bacterial genomes (Oliveira et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Oliveira et al., 2014.

claim: R–M systems protect bacteria by recognizing and degrading foreign phage DNA via methylation-specific site and restriction endonucleases (REases).
source: R–M systems protect bacteria self by recognizing and degrading foreign phage DNA via methylation-specific site and restriction endonucleases (REases) (Loenen et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Loenen et al., 2014b.

claim: The Pgl system only modifies the phage DNA in the first infection cycle, and cleaves phage DNA in the subsequent infections.
source: However, the Pgl only modifies the phage DNA in the first infection cycle, and cleaves phage DNA in the subsequent infections, which gives a warn to the neighboring cells (Hampton et al., 2020; Hoskisson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hampton et al., 2020 and Hoskisson et al., 2015.

claim: Phages have evolved strategies to counteract R–M and R–M-like systems, including unusual modifications such as hydroxymethylation, glycosylation, and glucosylation.
source: To counteract R–M and R–M-like systems, phages have evolved strategies, including unusual modifications such as hydroxymethylation, glycosylation, and glucosylation.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about phage-bacteria interactions.

claim: Phages can encode their own MTases to protect their DNA or employ strategies to evade restriction systems and other anti-RM defenses.
source: They can also encode their own MTases to protect their DNA or employ strategies to evade restriction systems and other anti-RM defenses (Vasu and Nagaraja, 2013; Murphy et al., 2013; Iida et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Vasu and Nagaraja, 2013; Murphy et al., 2013; and Iida et al., 1987.

claim: The epigenetic regulation of gene expression is highly prevalent among bacteria.
source: As more studies apply SMRT-seq to investigate bacterial methylomes, it has become evident that the epigenetic regulation of gene expression is highly prevalent among bacteria.
evidence: This is a general statement based on the growing body of SMRT-seq studies.

claim: The repertoire of MTases varies among P. syringae strains.
source: As the repertoire of MTases varies among P. syringae strains, this approach will help us to better understand the diversity of DNA methylation and epigenetic patterns among P. syringae species.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.
